query: What additive manufacturing strategy and post-processing route can enable the fabrication of a refractory high-entropy alloy family (Group IV-V transition metals) capable of retaining high-temperature structural integrity, and what specific microstructural state is hypothesized to optimize mechanical performance while mitigating the inherent brittleness associated with interstitial impurities?

generation.hypothesis: Fabrication of a Group IV-V transition metal refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW or WTaMoNbV) via Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF/SLM) followed by a specific post-processing route (e.g., hot isostatic pressing or solution annealing) can enable high-temperature structural integrity. The hypothesized optimal microstructural state is a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with a refined cellular/dendritic microstructure and minimized interstitial impurity segregation, which mitigates inherent brittleness while optimizing mechanical performance at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Mixed elemental powders of Group IV-V transition metals (Nb, Mo, Ta, W, V) with potential interstitial impurities (O, N, C)
generation.intervention: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF/SLM) using in-situ alloy formation from mixed elemental powders, followed by post-processing (e.g., Hot Isostatic Pressing or Solution Annealing)
generation.conditions: High-temperature service environment (e.g., >1000°C), additive manufacturing parameters optimized for complete fusion (e.g., linear energy density ~2.83 J/mm)
generation.structural_mediator: Single-phase BCC solid solution with refined cellular/dendritic microstructure and minimized interstitial segregation
generation.mechanism: Rapid solidification during LPBF suppresses intermetallic formation and refines microstructure; post-processing homogenizes composition and relieves residual stresses; single-phase BCC structure provides high-temperature stability and ductility; minimized interstitial impurity segregation reduces brittleness
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced high-temperature mechanical properties (strength, ductility, creep resistance) and structural integrity compared to conventionally processed alloys, with reduced brittleness due to optimized microstructure and impurity control
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed refractory HEAs (e.g., arc-melted) with coarse microstructures, potential intermetallic phases, and higher interstitial impurity content leading to brittleness
generation.boundary: Applicable to refractory HEAs based on Group IV-V transition metals (Nb, Mo, Ta, W, V); effectiveness may vary with specific alloy composition and processing parameters
generation.uncertainty: Optimal post-processing parameters and exact impurity thresholds for brittleness mitigation require further experimental validation; long-term high-temperature stability under cyclic loading needs confirmation
generation.falsification_experiment: Fabricate NbMoTaW alloy via LPBF with varying post-processing routes (HIP, annealing) and measure high-temperature mechanical properties (tensile, creep) and microstructure. Compare with conventionally processed alloy. Falsify if post-processed LPBF samples show no improvement in ductility or high-temperature strength, or if interstitial impurities remain segregated despite processing.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
